# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–40 + Epilogue (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 21)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Winter of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to Chapter 39 (autumn) to **Chapter 40 (winter; Imperial dinner day, Monday) to Epilogue (Imperial dinner evening and aftermath).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool, Conservative club in the City, Mount Street, Bond Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Salford; Yarlton; Salwick; Beccles (Suffolk); coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Salmere, Mirecombe, Miremere); harbor towns (Staveton, Salwick); Coldcombe hill farms; Commercial Road; Caversham; Vienna; Fenmere.

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn; **Epilogue: seen hale and well at summer fair in Mirecombe—contradicts prior report**). Feten Lindner followed her to Harrowgate within the month (likely died). Thidrek Corrett (**Epilogue: seen hale and well at summer fair in Fenmere despite gossips**).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. Chapter 39: Discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk. Suffering over his involvement with Marie Melmotte's elopement, money owed. Confessed troubles to Mr. Broune (Thursday evening). Received his counsel: must rid herself of Felix, extract money story, send word to him early next morning. Sent letter to Mr. Broune with Felix's account: claims Melmotte owed him £600; received £250 from Marie via Didon; lost this money at play. Acknowledged she cannot justify believing her son's account.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won substantial sums at gaming. **Chapter 38–39**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones"; attempted to meet Ruby at Music Hall but she did not appear. Between 6–7 A.M. Wednesday knocked at Welbeck Street door, drunk and sodden. Remained in bed through Friday morning. **Still in London as of Chapter 40; Marie realizes Sir Felix has not come for her; questions his pluck and truthfulness.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 39: Turned matter over in mind regarding marriage to one man while loving another.

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement

**Chapter 38**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes. Marie and Didon followed in second cab. Reached Euston Square, obtained tickets in French, departed. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM.** Gentleman addressed her by name; insisted they return to London; telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. Marie taken home; boxes to follow.

**Chapter 39**: Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking. Marie determined: "I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." Melmotte angry at Sir Felix beyond measure; would prosecute if possible. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune. Wrote to Lord Nidderdale, making clear breast of matter; urged him to renew suit.

**Chapter 40**: Nidderdale renewed suit in drawing-room at Grosvenor Square. Marie passionately rejected him: "If we had cared for each other they couldn't have broken it off... You never cared for me a bit." Broke down sobbing, confessed loves Sir Felix Carbury more than any person in world. Upon leaving, Nidderdale reflected he had "prospered, considering the extreme difficulties," thought her "quite a different sort of girl." Marie afterward walked about room almost in dismay, realizing Sir Felix not entirely as nice as thought him; questions why he does not come, why he does not show pluck, why he does not tell truth.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Chapter 39**: Paul wrote to Mrs. Hurtle acknowledging circumstances made their lives too different for happy marriage; broke engagement before knowing this girl; no grounds for hoping love will lead to results. **Mrs. Hurtle's Response**: Suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. Desired him to come with horsewhip in hand; threatened to whip him till has not breath in body. **Paul Meeting**: Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment. Spoke softly, then raised voice about his changing mind. Said: "I should still take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion." Asked advice what to do next; has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Paul suggested she remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin. Mrs. Pipkin went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Then absolute silence for minute. She handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip, then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft—softer letter. She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment... There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?" Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me... You do not love me." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you... Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?" **After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle announced standing upright: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague." She has decided to depart from Islington.**

## Augustus Melmotte and Imperial Dinner Crisis

**Chapter 39**: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, ignorant of elopement plot. Interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her. By two o'clock matter known to everybody. Anger against Sir Felix infinitely more bitter than against his daughter. Invited Lord Nidderdale to lunch at Conservative club; urged him to visit Grosvenor Square Sunday morning to renew suit.

**Imperial Reception Confrontation**: Stood directly in way of Secretary of State, demanded presentation to Emperor. Insisted: "It is generally understood... that the Emperor is to do me the honour of dining at my poor house on Monday." Threatened: "There shall be no dinner. I'll be d---- if any of the lot shall dine in Grosvenor Square on Monday." Under secretary Lord De Griffin intervened; Melmotte followed. **Had gained his point.**

**FORGERY RUMORS AND PICKERING PROPERTY CRISIS (Chapter 40 - CRITICAL)**: Horrid rumours prevailing in the City and spreading westwards to the House of Commons. Word "forgery" whispered by more than one pair of lips. Rumour particular: inferred the forgery to Melmotte's mode of acquiring the Pickering property. **Pickering estate had been already mortgaged by Melmotte to its full value at an assurance office.** **Houses in the East-end of London said bought and sold without payment of purchase money as to the buying, and with receipt as to the selling. Squercum had seen the letter in Mr. Bideawhile's office which conveyed to the father's lawyer the son's sanction for the surrender of the title-deeds. That letter, prepared in Bideawhile's office, purported to have Dolly's signature.** Signature, though scrawled as Dolly always scrawled it, was not like the scrawl of a drunken man. **Squercum quite sure that his client had not signed the letter. Dolly's manner on this occasion qualified to convince.** Mr. Squercum had been at work for above a week. **Other facts coming to light: great many shares of the South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway had been thrown upon the market, all passed through hands of Mr. Cohenlupe.** Then the mortgage of Pickering property, for which money certainly had not been paid; and traffic with half a street of houses near the Commercial Road, by which large sum of money had come into Melmotte's hands.

**Impact on Imperial Dinner Attendance**: **The Lord Mayor had made up his mind he would not go to the dinner. Melmotte was a commercial man, and as these were commercial transactions it behoved the Lord Mayor of London to be more careful than other men.** Others of the chosen few of the City resolved upon absenting themselves unless the Lord Mayor went. **No less than six declared City defaulters. At the last moment a seventh was taken ill and sent a note to Miles Grendall excusing himself.**

**Political Leadership Response**: **Prime Minister stated: "I should not feel myself justified in acting upon such a report... The dinner must certainly go on."** Political antagonist declared he would not desert his honourable friend;--but he could not answer for his followers. Strong feeling among Conservative party of distrust in Melmotte. **At that moment even the Prime Minister was much disturbed in his mind; but in such emergencies a Prime Minister can only choose the least of two evils. To have taken the Emperor to dine with a swindler would be very bad; but to desert him, and to stop the coming of the Emperor on a false rumour, would be worse.**

**The Imperial Dinner (Chapter 40 Evening)**: Servants and workmen giving admittance; wreaths of flowers and green boughs being suspended. Father Barham made his way to banqueting hall. Melmotte very angry indeed. Had been given to understand he was to sit opposite to Emperor. Now explained to him this could not be done. Melmotte's own seat became really quite obscure. Succeeded in having removed the bar which had been specially put up to prevent his intrusion on his own guests in his own house. Insisted Lord Alfred sit next to himself. **Melmotte repeatedly asked Lord Alfred why many guests were absent, glancing round the hall with anxiety. Lord Alfred replied surly.** **Melmotte knew from the old man's manner (and Lord Alfred's manner) that there was something each could tell him if he would, but he was unable to make the men open their mouths.** **The grand arrivals were fairly punctual, and the very grand people all came. The unfortunate Emperor, with impassible and awful dignity, was marshalled into the room on the ground floor. Melmotte, bowing to the ground, walked backwards before him. Princes had all shaken hands with host; Princesses had bowed graciously. Nothing of the rumour had been whispered in royal palaces. The company was very select. The Prime Minister, one archbishop, two duchesses, and an ex-governor of India were alone there.** **Father Barham walked close to scene of action. "Who the d---- are you?" Melmotte asked. Father Barham stood humbly with his hat off. "I am the Rev. Mr. Barham," said visitor. "I am the priest of Beccles in Suffolk."** Father Barham went away disgusted; yet not altogether disheartened. Man had not declared he was not Roman Catholic. Before he returned to Beccles, Father Barham made himself believe Mr. Melmotte was certainly Roman Catholic.

**Epilogue - Dinner Outcome**: **Sir Damask Monogram arrived past ten o'clock. On arriving in Grosvenor Square he could at once see that the party was going on. The house was illuminated. There was a concourse of servants round the door, and half the square was already blocked up with carriages. He saw the royal liveries. There was no doubt about the party. The Emperor and the Princes and the Princesses were all there. As far as Sir Damask could perceive, the dinner had been quite a success.** **Later, Lady Monogram and Sir Damask arrived at the house, found that the Emperor of China and all the Royalties had been there,--but had taken their departure.**

## Georgiana Longestaffe and Mr. Brehgert

**Chapter 40**: Georgiana asked Lady Monogram whether she would have Mr. Brehgert (presumably Jewish) to dinner. Lady Monogram declined, stating she maintains social lines and does not introduce "new-comers." Offered compromise: Georgiana could ask Mr. Brehgert to Tuesday evening gathering when rooms would be full. "So the matter was at last settled. Miss Longestaffe did ask Mr. Brehgert for the Tuesday evening, and the two ladies were again friends."

**Georgiana's Reasoning**: Georgiana reflected: "Lovers with all the glories and all the graces are supposed to be plentiful as blackberries by girls of nineteen, but have been proved to be rare hothouse fruits by girls of twenty-nine. Brehgert was rich, would live in London, and would be a husband. People did such odd things now and 'lived them down,' that she could see no reason why she should not do this and live this down. Courage was the one thing necessary,--that and perseverance."

**Epilogue - Engagement and Marriage Plans**: Before leaving the Melmottes in Bruton Street, Brehgert was with her. The Melmottes knew of the engagement and quite approved of it. Madame Melmotte rather aspired to credit for having had so happy an affair arranged under her auspices—set-off against Marie's unfortunate escapade. Brehgert pressed for an early day. **"I must at any rate ask mamma about it," said Georgiana.** Brehgert was satisfied with answer and went away promising he would meet his love at the great Melmotte reception. **She sat silent, thinking how she should declare the matter to her family. Would it not be better for her to say to them at once that there must be a division among them,--an absolute breaking off of all old ties, so that it should be tacitly acknowledged that she, Georgiana, had gone out from among the Longestaffes altogether, and had become one with the Melmottes, Brehgerts, and Goldsheiners?** It would be expedient that they should be married from the Melmottes' house, and the Melmottes would leave town some time in August. Unless married from the Melmottes' house, she must go down to Caversham for the occasion—which would be intolerable. If the spending of money could do it, it should be done.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway
Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway. Directorate: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Lord Nidderdale
That absurd elopement perhaps his strongest objection. By the Sunday evening he had determined that he would try again. Expected plum would fall into his mouth. Prospect of endless money.

## Roger Carbury and Father Barham
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Philosophical Discussion with Bishop: Roger discussed Melmotte's fitness for Parliament. **Father Barham at Carbury Manor**: Roof blown off Father Barham's cottage by wind; Roger offered him shelter while damage being repaired. Shelter much more comfortable than priest's own establishment; Father Barham in clover.

## Minor Characters
Didon (Marie's attendant, executed elopement plan). Miles Grendall (Secretary to Melmotte; does not pay debts of honour; thrust note of City defaulter into his hands just as Emperor arrived). Robert (Marie's servant; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes). Lord Alfred Grendall (absolutely dependent on Melmotte; born and bred gentleman; found position almost insupportable). Dolly Longestaffe (parent of forgery rumor via attorney Squercum).
